mainTopic: Damaging קדשים, and explaining the phrases of the משנה: בני ברית, נכסים המיוחדין, the מזיק's domain, the shared courtyard and שומרים
overview: The amud opens by finishing a point about a damaging שלמים: the ניזק cannot say that only the meat did the damage and not the אימורין. רבא then rules that from a damaging תודה the ניזק collects from the meat but not the bread. The גמרא explains that the real point is that the owner must still bring the bread, because it is his own obligation. Next the גמרא explains phrases of the משנה. 'בני ברית' excludes a גוי's property. 'נכסים המיוחדין' gets three explanations: an unclear case where each owner blames the other's ox, an ownerless ox (from a ברייתא), or, according to רבינא, an ox that was made הקדש or הפקר after it gored. A ברייתא of רבי יהודה supports רבינא: the ox's status must be the same at the death, the trial and the verdict. Then the גמרא explains why there is no liability in the מזיק's own domain. רב חסדא and רבי אלעזר disagree about a shared courtyard, and each reads the משנה differently. Finally, the גמרא brings a ברייתא that makes the four kinds of שומרים liable for damage done by an animal in their care. It starts working out the exact case, which continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The whole animal did the damage, not just the meat
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finishes a distinction. In our case of a damaging שלמים, the ניזק cannot argue that only the meat caused damage and the אימורין did not.
steps.simpleTranslation: But here, can he really say: 'The meat did damage, the sacrificial parts did not do damage'?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is closing an argument from just before this line. It explains why our case is different from the case it was compared to.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ניזק wants to collect from the meat of a damaging שלמים. The meat belongs to the owner, but the אימורין go on the מזבח. Since the entire animal caused the damage, the ניזק cannot pretend the damage came only from the meat. So he cannot collect the full damage from the meat alone.

keyTerms.meaning: The parts of a קרבן that are burned on the מזבח
Can he really say? (a question that expects the answer 'no')
Did damage
Here, in our case

steps.confusionAlert: This line is the end of an argument that started before this text. 'Here' means the case of a damaging קדשים קלים animal, and it is being set against a different case mentioned just before.

phrases.english: But here,
can he really say:
'The meat did damage, the sacrificial parts did not do damage'?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes a distinction that began before this text
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the cases: the whole animal did the damage
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We might have thought the ניזק could treat the meat alone as the damager and collect everything from it
steps.terutzMaskana: He cannot split the animal, because the אימורין were part of the animal that did the damage

steps.title: A damaging תודה: collect from the meat, not the bread
steps.stepSummary: רבא rules that if a תודה animal caused damage, the ניזק collects from its meat but not from its bread.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: A תודה that caused damage, he collects from its meat, and he does not collect from its bread.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives a new rule about a תודה, which is a kind of קדשים קלים that comes with loaves of bread.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Like a שלמים, the meat of a תודה can be eaten by the owner, so the ניזק can collect from it. The bread that comes along with the תודה is a separate item. The ניזק cannot collect from it.

keyTerms.meaning: A thanks-offering, brought together with loaves of bread
Collects payment
Its bread, the loaves that come with the תודה

phrases.english: Rava said:
A thanks-offering that caused damage,
he collects from its meat,
and he does not collect from its bread.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the rule about damaging קדשים קלים to a תודה
steps.mimraCoreRuling: From a damaging תודה, the ניזק collects from the meat but not from the bread

steps.title: Isn't it obvious about the bread?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why רבא needed to say that the ניזק doesn't collect from the bread. That seems obvious.
steps.simpleTranslation: The bread? That is obvious!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבא's rule as saying something too obvious to need saying.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The bread is not part of the animal and did no damage. So of course the ניזק cannot collect from it. Why would רבא need to teach it?

keyTerms.meaning: It is obvious, so why say it?
Bread

phrases.english: The bread? That is obvious!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the need for רבא's statement
steps.kashyaTarget: The second half of רבא's rule: 'he does not collect from its bread'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The bread did no damage, so this part of the rule teaches nothing new

steps.title: רבא needed the second half: the owner still brings the bread
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that רבא's rule was needed for its last part: the ניזק eats the meat, and the owner still must bring the bread.
steps.simpleTranslation: He needed the last part: the injured party eats the meat, and the one getting atonement brings the bread.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the new point in רבא's rule. It is not just that the ניזק can't take the bread. The owner still has to supply it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: We might think that once the ניזק takes the meat, the owner has no duty to bring the bread. רבא teaches that the owner still brings the bread with the קרבן, while the ניזק eats the meat as payment.

keyTerms.meaning: The last part of a statement
He needed it, it was necessary to say
The injured party
The one who gets atonement through the קרבן, meaning the owner

steps.whatToRemember: From a damaging תודה, the ניזק eats the meat as payment, but the owner still has to bring the loaves of bread.

phrases.english: He needed it for the last part:
the injured party eats the meat,
and the one getting atonement brings the bread.
phrases.notes: That's the owner of the תודה.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the פשיטא challenge
steps.terutzResolutionType: The real point is in the last part of the rule
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We might think the owner no longer has to bring the bread once the ניזק takes the meat
steps.terutzMaskana: The ניזק eats the meat, and the owner still brings the bread

steps.title: Isn't the owner bringing the bread also obvious?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the answer from step 4: it seems obvious that the owner still has to bring the bread.
steps.simpleTranslation: This too is obvious!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the answer from step 4. It says the 'last part' of רבא's rule (the owner still brings the bread) is also obvious, so why say it?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 4 said רבא's rule was needed for its last part: the ניזק eats the meat and the owner brings the bread. Now the גמרא says even that is obvious. The ניזק has no connection to the קרבן, so who else would bring the bread?

keyTerms.meaning: This too, this also
It is obvious, so why does it need to be said?

phrases.english: This too is obvious!
phrases.notes: 'This' is the last part of רבא's rule from step 4: the owner still has to bring the bread.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer given in step 4.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer in step 4, that רבא's ruling was needed to teach that the owner still brings the bread.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Obviously the owner, whose קרבן it is, brings the bread. Saying so adds nothing, so it cannot be why רבא spoke.

steps.title: Without רבא, the owner might have pushed the bread onto the ניזק
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains the mistake רבא was preventing. Since the bread makes the תודה valid, the owner might have told the ניזק to bring the bread himself. רבא teaches that the bread is the owner's own obligation.
steps.simpleTranslation: You might have said: since the bread is what makes the offering valid, the owner can tell the ניזק, 'You are eating the meat, and I should bring the bread?' So רבא teaches us that the bread is the owner's obligation.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. It shows that the owner bringing the bread is not obvious, because there was a real reason to think otherwise.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The bread is needed to make the תודה complete and valid. So one might think whoever gets the meat should also cover the bread. רבא teaches that the bread is a personal obligation of the owner, not something tied to whoever eats the meat.

keyTerms.meaning: You might have said (the mistaken idea the ruling prevents)
What makes the offering valid and complete
So it teaches us
The owner's own obligation

steps.whatToRemember: The bread of a תודה is the owner's personal obligation. Even when the ניזק collects the meat, the owner must still bring the bread.

phrases.english: You might have said,
since the bread is what makes the offering valid –
let him say to him:
phrases.notes: The owner of the תודה is talking to the ניזק, the one who collected the meat.

phrases.aramaic: אַתְּ אָכְלַתְּ בְּשַׂר, וַאֲנָא אַיְיתֵי לֶחֶם;
phrases.english: you eat the meat, and I should bring the bread?
So it teaches us
that the bread is the obligation of the owner.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 5.
steps.terutzResolutionType: מהו דתימא: shows there was a reasonable mistaken idea that the ruling had to rule out.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since the bread makes the תודה valid, the owner could tell the ניזק who eats the meat to bring the bread too.
steps.terutzMaskana: The bread is the owner's personal obligation, so the owner must bring it.

steps.title: What does 'property of בני ברית' exclude?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's phrase 'property of בני ברית' and asks what it excludes. If it excludes a גוי's property, a later משנה already says that, so why say it here?
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: 'Property that belongs to בני ברית.' What does this exclude? If it excludes a גוי's property, the משנה teaches that later: an ox of a Jew that gored an ox of a גוי is exempt!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the opening משנה and quotes a new phrase. It asks what the phrase comes to exclude, and points out that the obvious answer seems to repeat a later משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The phrase 'בני ברית' seems to exclude a גוי's property. But a later משנה already says that a Jew's ox that gores a גוי's ox is exempt. A משנה should not say the same thing twice for no reason, so the phrase here looks extra.

keyTerms.meaning: Property, belongings
Members of the covenant (Jews)
What does it come to exclude?
Later on, further ahead
Exempt, does not have to pay

phrases.english: Property that belongs to members of the covenant.
To exclude what?
If to exclude that of a גוי –
it is taught later on:
phrases.notes: This points to a later משנה in this מסכת, on 37b.

phrases.aramaic: שׁוֹר שֶׁל יִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁנָּגַח שׁוֹר שֶׁל גּוֹי – פָּטוּר!
phrases.english: an ox of a Jew that gored an ox of a גוי – exempt!

steps.triggerLanguage: לְמַעוֹטֵי מַאי? אִי לְמַעוֹטֵי דְּגוֹי – הָא קָתָנֵי לַהּ לְקַמַּן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the תודה discussion and returns to analyzing the wording of the opening משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: The phrase 'נכסים שהן של בני ברית' in our משנה.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the phrase excludes a גוי's property, it repeats a later משנה that already says so. That makes it seem extra.

steps.title: The משנה states the rule first and explains it later
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the משנה gives the rule briefly here and explains it in detail later. This is a normal way for a משנה to teach.
steps.simpleTranslation: It teaches it, and then it explains it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. The repetition is not a problem, because the משנה is stating a general rule now and spelling it out later.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The phrase here does exclude a גוי's property. It is not an extra repeat, because a משנה often states a rule briefly and then gives the details later. The later משנה is the detailed explanation of this short rule.

keyTerms.meaning: It teaches, and then it explains

phrases.english: It teaches, and then explains.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 7.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Style of the משנה: a short general rule first, details later.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The phrase 'בני ברית' looks like a needless repeat of the later משנה.
steps.terutzMaskana: The phrase does exclude a גוי's property. The משנה states it in general here and explains it later.

steps.title: What does 'assigned property' exclude?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's next phrase, 'נכסים המיוחדין' (property belonging to a specific owner), and asks what it excludes.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: 'Assigned property.' What does this exclude?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes another phrase from the משנה and asks what it comes to leave out. This step sets up רב יהודה's answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a plain question, not an attack. The גמרא assumes every phrase in the משנה teaches something. Here it wants to know which case 'assigned property' leaves out.

keyTerms.meaning: Assigned, belonging to a specific known person

phrases.english: Assigned property.
phrases.notes: Again the גמרא is quoting our משנה. 'Assigned' means the property clearly belongs to one known person.

phrases.english: To exclude what?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to the next phrase of the משנה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which case the phrase 'נכסים המיוחדין' comes to exclude.

steps.title: רב יהודה: it excludes when each owner blames the other's ox
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה says the phrase excludes a case where it is unclear whose ox did the damage, and each owner says, 'Your ox did it.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said: It excludes a case where this one says, 'Your ox did the damage,' and that one says, 'Your ox did the damage.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב יהודה answers the question from step 9. He explains which case 'assigned property' leaves out.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is only liability when the damaging animal is known to belong to a specific owner. If two owners each blame the other's ox and no one can prove whose ox did it, the damager is not 'assigned' to anyone. So neither owner is made to pay.

keyTerms.meaning: An אמורא who gives the answer here
Your ox
Did damage

steps.whatToRemember: 'נכסים המיוחדין' means the damaging animal must be known to belong to a specific owner. When two owners each blame the other's ox and it cannot be proven, there is no one to hold liable.
steps.confusionAlert: Here 'assigned property' is about the ox that did the damage, not the damaged property. The question is whose ox caused the harm.

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said:
To exclude where this one says, 'Your ox did the damage,'
phrases.notes: Picture two oxen near a damaged animal, and no one knows which ox did it.

phrases.english: and that one says, 'Your ox did the damage.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 9.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The phrase excludes a case where it is unclear whose ox caused the damage and each owner blames the other. Since the damager is not known to be a specific person's ox, no one is liable.

steps.title: A later משנה already teaches the two-oxen case
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רב יהודה. A later משנה already says that when two oxen chase one, and each owner blames the other, both owners are exempt. So why would our משנה hint at the same case?
steps.simpleTranslation: But a later משנה already teaches this: if two oxen were chasing one ox, and each owner says 'Your ox did the damage,' both are exempt!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks רב יהודה's answer from Step 10. The case he describes is already taught openly in a later משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב יהודה said 'נכסים המיוחדין' excludes the case where we don't know whose ox did the damage. But that exact case appears later in the מסכת. The משנה does not normally repeat itself for no reason, so his reading looks unnecessary.

keyTerms.meaning: later on, further ahead in the text
chasing
your ox did the damage
exempt from paying

phrases.english: But it is taught later on:
If two oxen were chasing after one ox,
this owner says: 'Your ox did the damage,'
and that owner says: 'Your ox did the damage' —
both of them are exempt!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב יהודה's answer in Step 10
steps.kashyaTarget: רב יהודה's reading that 'נכסים המיוחדין' excludes a case where it is unclear whose ox did the damage
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A later משנה already teaches this case openly, so reading it into our משנה would make the משנה repeat itself

steps.title: The משנה states the rule here and explains it later
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the משנה first gives the rule briefly and then spells it out in detail later.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה teaches the rule here, and later it explains it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רב יהודה with the same kind of answer it gave in Step 8.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Saying a rule in general terms and later explaining it in detail is not real repetition. So רב יהודה's reading can stand.

keyTerms.meaning: it teaches, and then explains

steps.confusionAlert: This is the same answer as in Step 8, now used for a different phrase in the משנה. It is a standard pattern, not a mistake.

phrases.english: It teaches the rule, and then explains it later.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 11
steps.terutzResolutionType: Teaching style: a brief rule first, a detailed explanation later
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Our משנה would be repeating the later משנה for no reason
steps.terutzMaskana: The brief mention here and the detailed one later are a normal teaching pattern, so רב יהודה's reading holds

steps.title: A ברייתא: the phrase excludes ownerless property
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא gives a different answer: 'נכסים המיוחדין' excludes property that belongs to no one (הפקר).
steps.simpleTranslation: A ברייתא teaches: this excludes ownerless property.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second answer to the question from Step 9, this time from a ברייתא. It says the phrase excludes ownerless (הפקר) property.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Property that belongs to a specific owner is the opposite of property that belongs to no one. So the ברייתא reads the phrase as leaving out damage connected to הפקר.

keyTerms.meaning: here, a ברייתא: a teaching of the תנאים outside the משנה
to exclude, leaving out
ownerless property

phrases.english: It was taught in a ברייתא:
phrases.notes: Here מתניתא doesn't mean our משנה; it means a ברייתא.

phrases.english: to exclude ownerless property.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a different answer than רב יהודה to the question of Step 9

steps.title: Which case of ownerless property is meant?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what case the ברייתא means. If our ox gored an ownerless ox, that is obvious, since nobody owns the hurt ox and nobody can demand payment.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the case? If you say our ox gored an ownerless ox, who would claim payment from him?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries to picture the case behind the ברייתא. It rejects the first option, because nobody would even sue.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the hurt ox belongs to no one, there is no ניזק to demand payment. So the ברייתא would not need to teach that case, and it must mean something else.

keyTerms.meaning: what is the case? how does it look?
if you say
our ox, an ox owned by a Jew
who is claiming from him?

phrases.english: What is the case?
If you say that our ox gored
an ownerless ox —
who is claiming payment from him?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks which case the ברייתא in Step 13 means
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which case of ownerless property the ברייתא is excluding

steps.title: An ownerless ox gored our ox
steps.stepSummary: So the case must be that an ownerless ox gored our ox, and the ברייתא teaches that nobody has to pay.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it is where an ownerless ox gored our ox.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא settles on the second option: the ox that did the damage is ownerless.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here there is a real ניזק but no owner who is responsible for the damage. The ברייתא tells us the ניזק cannot collect payment.

keyTerms.meaning: rather
gored

phrases.english: Rather, where an ownerless ox gored
our ox —

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 14
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The ox that did the damage is ownerless, and the injured ox belongs to a Jew

steps.title: He can just take the ownerless ox
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: if the ox that did the damage is ownerless, the ניזק can simply go and take it for himself. So what does the ברייתא add?
steps.simpleTranslation: Let him go and take it!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the case from Step 15. The hurt party can make up his loss by taking the ownerless ox.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Ownerless property can be taken by anyone. So saying 'no payment' seems pointless, because the ניזק can just grab the ox.

keyTerms.meaning: let him go and take it

phrases.english: Let him go and take it for himself!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the case set up in Step 15
steps.kashyaTarget: The need for the ברייתא to exclude damage done by an ownerless ox
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ניזק can acquire the ownerless ox himself, so the rule seems to make no difference

steps.title: Someone else took the ox first
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the case is where another person acquired the ownerless ox first. The ניזק then has no claim against the new owner.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is where someone else got there first and acquired it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא narrows the case. A different person already took the ownerless ox before the ניזק could.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The new owner did not own the ox when it gored. So the ניזק cannot demand payment from him or take the ox away from him.

keyTerms.meaning: got there first
acquired it
another person

steps.whatToRemember: According to the ברייתא, 'נכסים המיוחדין' excludes damage by an ownerless ox, even if someone else acquired it afterward.

phrases.english: Where another person got there first and acquired it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 16
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ניזק could just take the ownerless ox, so the rule teaches nothing
steps.terutzMaskana: Someone else acquired the ox first, and the ניזק has no claim against him

steps.title: רבינא: the ox gored and was then made הקדש or הפקר
steps.stepSummary: רבינא gives another answer: the phrase excludes an ox that gored, and afterward its owner made it הקדש or declared it הפקר.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא said: it excludes where the ox gored and afterward the owner made it הקדש, or where it gored and afterward the owner made it ownerless.
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא offers a third answer to what 'נכסים המיוחדין' excludes. It covers an ox that had an owner when it gored but lost that owner afterward.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Unlike the ברייתא, here the ox did have an owner at the time of the damage. רבינא teaches that the ox must also belong to an owner later, when the case is judged, or there is no payment.

keyTerms.meaning: an אמורא who gives a third answer
to exclude
he dedicated it to the בית המקדש (הקדש)
he declared it ownerless

steps.whatToRemember: Three answers for 'נכסים המיוחדין': רב יהודה says it means unclear whose ox did the damage; the ברייתא says an ownerless ox; רבינא says the owner gave up the ox after it gored.
steps.whyThisMatters: רבינא's answer shows that ownership matters at two points: when the ox does the damage and when the case comes to court.

phrases.english: רבינא said:
It excludes where it gored and afterward the owner dedicated it to the Temple;
or where it gored and afterward the owner made it ownerless.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a third answer to the question of Step 9, different from רב יהודה and the ברייתא
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: An ox that gored and was then made הקדש or declared הפקר, so it has no owner when the case is judged

steps.title: A ברייתא supports רבינא: goring followed by הקדש or הפקר is exempt
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא quotes רבי יהודה: even if the ox gored first and only afterward was made הקדש or הפקר, the case is פטור. He learns this from the פסוק 'והועד בבעליו והמית איש,' which teaches that the ox's status at the time of the death and at the time of the court case must be the same.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is also taught this way in a ברייתא: Moreover, רבי יהודה said: Even if the ox gored and afterward the owner made it הקדש, or gored and afterward the owner made it הפקר, it is פטור. This is because the פסוק says 'and its owner was warned... and it killed a man.' The ox's status at the death and at the standing in court must be the same.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that backs up רבינא's answer from the previous step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבינא said the phrase excludes an ox that gored and then became הקדש or הפקר. רבי יהודה rules exactly that way. His source is the פסוק mentioning the owner (בבעליו): the ox must be in the same ownership both when the person died and when the case comes to court. If ownership changed in between, there is no case.

keyTerms.meaning: It is also taught this way: a ברייתא that supports what was just said
Moreover; going even further than the earlier ruling
He made it holy property, given to the בית המקדש
He gave up ownership, making it ownerless
Standing in court; when the case is brought to בית דין
The same at both times

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that the ox's ownership at the time of judgment matters, not only at the time of the damage.

phrases.english: It is also taught this way in a ברייתא:

phrases.aramaic: יָתֵר עַל כֵּן אָמַר רַבִּי יְהוּדָה:
phrases.english: Moreover, Rabbi Yehuda said:
Even if it gored and afterward the owner made it הקדש,
or it gored and afterward he made it ownerless, it is exempt,
as it says: "and its owner had been warned
and it killed a man, etc."
unless the death and the standing in court
are the same together.
phrases.notes: He means the ox must have the same owner both when the person dies and when the case comes to court.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a ברייתא supporting רבינא's answer in step 18.
steps.raayaObject: רבינא's claim that an ox that gored and was then made הקדש or הפקר is excluded.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא of רבי יהודה, based on the פסוק 'והועד בבעליו והמית איש' (שמות 21:29).

steps.title: Isn't the final verdict needed too?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the wording of the ברייתא. It mentions only the death and the standing in court. But the פסוק 'השור יסקל' refers to the final verdict, so the verdict should matter too.
steps.simpleTranslation: And don't we also need the final verdict? But 'the ox shall be stoned' is written about the final verdict!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out that the ברייתא's rule seems to leave something out.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא lists two times that must match: the death and the court hearing. The words 'השור יסקל' describe what happens at the final verdict. So the verdict is also a key moment, and the ox's status then should matter as well.

keyTerms.meaning: The final verdict of the court
Don't we need?
The ox shall be stoned

phrases.english: And don't we need the final verdict too?!
But "the ox shall be stoned"
is written about the final verdict!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the wording of the ברייתא just quoted.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's phrase 'מיתה והעמדה בדין שוין כאחד.'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The פסוק 'השור יסקל' refers to the final verdict, so the verdict should also be a time when the status must match.

steps.title: Reword the rule to include the final verdict
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers by rewording the ברייתא. The death, the standing in court, and the final verdict must all share the same status.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, say: unless the death, the standing in court, and the final verdict are all the same.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא fixes the ברייתא's wording so that it includes the final verdict.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Nothing about רבי יהודה's ruling changes, only the wording. Now three moments must match: the death, the court hearing, and the verdict. If the ox becomes הקדש or הפקר at any point before the verdict, it is פטור.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather, say: the גמרא rewords a source

steps.whatToRemember: For the ox to be judged, it must have the same ownership status at three moments: the death, the court hearing, and the final verdict.

phrases.english: Rather, say:
unless the death and the standing in court
and the final verdict are all the same together.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 20 by rewording the ברייתא.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא required only the death and the standing in court to match.
steps.terutzMaskana: The final verdict must also match, so there are three moments in all.

steps.title: Why there is no payment in the damager's own domain
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא moves to a new phrase in the משנה: 'except for a domain set aside for the מזיק.' The reason is that the owner of the property can say to the ניזק: 'What was your ox doing on my property?'
steps.simpleTranslation: Except for a domain set aside for the damager, because he can say to him: What was your ox doing in my domain?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic. It quotes the next phrase of the משנה and gives the reason behind it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה makes the מזיק liable in most places, but not on his own private property. The reason is that the hurt animal had no right to be there. The owner does not have to guard his animal on his own land against animals that come in without permission.

keyTerms.meaning: A domain set aside only for the one who caused the damage
Your ox
What was it doing? What business did it have there?

steps.whyThisMatters: It sets a basic principle in נזיקין: a person is not responsible for damage his animal does on his own property to an animal that came in without permission.

phrases.english: Except for a domain set aside for the one who caused the damage.
Because he can say to him:
What was your ox doing in my domain?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the הקדש and הפקר discussion and moves on to the next phrase of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: There is no liability in the damager's own domain, because the hurt animal had no right to be there.

steps.title: In a shared courtyard the owner is liable for שן and רגל
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the next phrase of the משנה, 'ורשות הניזק והמזיק.' רב חסדא in the name of אבימי rules that in a חצר השותפין one is חייב for שן and רגל. So the phrase starts a new clause: in a shared domain, the מזיק pays.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says: 'And a domain of the injured party and the damager.' רב חסדא said in the name of אבימי: In a courtyard owned by partners, the owner is liable for Tooth and Foot damage done there. So the משנה means: 'Except for a domain set aside for the damager,' where he is exempt. 'But in a domain shared by the injured party and the damager, when it damages, the damager must pay.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the next words of the משנה and brings רב חסדא's ruling that in a shared courtyard you must pay for שן and רגל damage. It then shows how this ruling changes the way we read the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For שן and רגל, one is פטור in the public domain and חייב in the ניזק's own domain. A shared courtyard is partly the ניזק's own place, so the ניזק cannot be told 'What was your ox doing here?' According to this view, 'ורשות הניזק והמזיק' is not part of the exemption list. It opens the clause that ends with 'חב המזיק.'

keyTerms.meaning: A courtyard owned jointly by partners
'Tooth': damage done when an animal eats for its own benefit
'Foot': damage done when an animal tramples as it walks normally
'And this is what it is saying': introduces a reading of the משנה's words
The damager is obligated to pay

steps.confusionAlert: The same words of the משנה can be split two ways. Here 'ורשות הניזק והמזיק' is joined to the words AFTER it (liable). In the next step it is joined to the words BEFORE it (exempt). Keep track of where the line is drawn.

phrases.english: And a domain of the injured party and the damager.
Rav Chisda said that Avimi said:
A courtyard of partners —

phrases.aramaic: חַיָּיב בָּהּ עַל הַשֵּׁן וְעַל הָרֶגֶל.
phrases.english: one is liable in it for Tooth and for Foot.
And this is what it [the Mishnah] is saying:
'Except for a domain set aside for the damager' — where he is exempt;
'but a domain of the injured party and the damager —
when it damages, the damager is obligated.'
phrases.notes: In this reading, the words 'and a domain of the injured party and the damager' go with this clause, so the shared courtyard is a place where he pays.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא אָמַר אֲבִימִי: חֲצַר הַשּׁוּתָּפִין – חַיָּיב בָּהּ עַל הַשֵּׁן וְעַל הָרֶגֶל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues through the משנה phrase by phrase. Step 22 explained the private domain of the מזיק, and this step explains the next phrase about a shared domain.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In a חצר השותפין one is חייב for שן and רגל. So 'ורשות הניזק והמזיק' begins the liability clause.

steps.title: רבי אלעזר says a shared courtyard is exempt, and the last clause adds קרן
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר disagrees: in a חצר השותפין one is פטור for שן and רגל. So 'ורשות הניזק והמזיק' belongs to the list of exemptions, and the final clause 'כשהזיק חב המזיק' comes to include קרן.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלעזר said: In a shared courtyard, one is exempt for Tooth and Foot. So the משנה means: 'Except for a domain set aside for the damager, and a domain of the injured party and the damager,' which is also exempt. And the words 'when it damages, the damager is obligated' come to include Goring.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אלעזר gives the opposite ruling about a shared courtyard and reads the משנה differently. He also gives the last clause a new job: teaching that the owner pays for קרן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבי אלעזר, a shared courtyard counts like the מזיק's own place as far as שן and רגל go, so the owner is פטור. That makes the משנה list two exempt places. The closing words 'חב המזיק' are no longer needed for the shared courtyard, so he says they add קרן (goring), for which one is liable even in the shared courtyard.

keyTerms.meaning: Exempt from paying
'Horn': damage done by goring, done on purpose to harm
'To include': this wording comes to add another case
Also

phrases.english: And Rabbi Elazar said:
He is exempt for Tooth and for Foot.
phrases.notes: He is talking about the same shared courtyard from the previous step.

phrases.english: And this is what it is saying:
'Except for a domain set aside for the damager,
and a domain of the injured party and the damager' — also exempt;
'and when it damages, the damager is obligated' —
comes to include Goring.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר אָמַר: פָּטוּר עַל הַשֵּׁן וְעַל הָרֶגֶל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the opposing ruling to רב חסדא and reads the משנה differently.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In a חצר השותפין one is פטור for שן and רגל. 'ורשות הניזק והמזיק' is a second exemption, and 'חב המזיק' comes to include קרן.

steps.title: According to רב, what does 'the damager is obligated' add?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבי אלעזר's reading. Saying the last clause adds קרן works for שמואל, who said 'שור' in the first משנה means רגל. But רב said 'שור' already includes everything an ox does, קרן too. So according to רב, what does 'חב המזיק' come to include?
steps.simpleTranslation: This works well for שמואל. But according to רב, who said the משנה taught 'ox' to mean an ox and all the kinds of damage an ox does, what does 'the damager is obligated' come to include?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a difficulty with רבי אלעזר's reading. It works for one side of an earlier argument between רב and שמואל, but seems not to work for the other side.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier, on 3b, רב and שמואל argued about the word 'שור' in the first משנה of the פרק. For שמואל it means רגל, so קרן has not been mentioned yet, and 'חב המזיק' can add it. For רב, 'שור' already covers קרן, שן and רגל. That leaves the clause with nothing new to teach under רבי אלעזר's reading.

keyTerms.meaning: 'It works well': opens a challenge that fits one view but not another
'It taught ox and all matters of an ox': רב's view that 'שור' covers every kind of ox damage
'To include what?': what new case does this wording add?

steps.confusionAlert: This question is aimed at רבי אלעזר's reading, not at רב חסדא's. For רב חסדא, 'חב המזיק' already has a job: making him liable in the shared courtyard.

phrases.english: This works well according to Shmuel,
phrases.notes: Back on 3b, שמואל said 'שור' in the first משנה means Foot, so Goring hadn't been taught yet.

phrases.english: but according to Rav, who said:
it taught 'ox' and all matters of an ox,
'the damager is obligated' comes to include what?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks רבי אלעזר's claim in step 24 that 'חב המזיק' comes to include קרן.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי אלעזר's reading that 'כשהזיק חב המזיק' comes to include קרן.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: According to רב, the word 'שור' in the first משנה already includes קרן. So 'חב המזיק' would add nothing new, and a phrase in the משנה cannot be left with no purpose.

steps.title: The last clause brings in the ברייתא about watchmen
steps.stepSummary: According to רב, 'כשהזיק חב המזיק' comes to include a ברייתא: the שומר חנם, שואל, נושא שכר and שוכר are responsible when an animal in their care does damage. A תם pays half and a מועד pays full. If the animal broke out through no fault of theirs, they are פטור.
steps.simpleTranslation: It comes to include what the Rabbis taught: 'When it damaged, the one responsible for the damage is liable.' This includes an unpaid watchman, a borrower, a paid watchman and a renter, when an animal did damage while in their care. If it is a תם, he pays half damages. If it is a מועד, he pays full damages. If the wall broke open at night, or bandits broke it open, and the animal went out and did damage, he is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from Step 25. Even for רב, the words 'חב המזיק' are not extra. They teach that whoever is watching the animal, not only the owner, is the one who pays for its damage.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'המזיק' here means 'the one responsible for the damage', not only the owner. So a person who took on the job of watching the animal steps into the owner's shoes and pays the usual amounts: half for a תם, full for a מועד. If the animal escaped only because of a break-in or a wall that collapsed at night, the watchman did nothing wrong and is פטור.

keyTerms.meaning: An unpaid watchman, someone who guards an item or animal as a favor.
A borrower, someone who uses another person's item for free.
A paid watchman.
A renter, someone who pays to use another person's item.
Bandits or robbers.

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the basic rule that responsibility for an animal's damage moves to whoever is watching it. The rest of this section tries to work out exactly what case that rule is talking about.

phrases.english: To include that which the Rabbis taught:
phrases.notes: This answers the question from Step 25: what does 'חב המזיק' add according to רב?

phrases.english: "When it damaged, the one responsible for the damage is liable"
to include an unpaid watchman and the borrower,
a paid watchman and the renter,
where an animal did damage while in their care;
if it is a תם, he pays half damages,
and if it is a מועד, he pays full damages.
If the wall broke open at night
or bandits broke it open,
and it went out and did damage, he is exempt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of Step 25 by finding a new thing for the clause to include according to רב.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Gives the clause a different job: it includes watchmen, not קרן.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: According to רב the clause 'חב המזיק' seemed to have nothing left to include.
steps.terutzMaskana: The clause teaches that the four kinds of שומרים pay when an animal in their care does damage.

steps.title: What case is the ברייתא talking about?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the start of the ברייתא again and asks what exact case it means.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Master said: 'When it damaged, the one responsible for the damage is liable', to include an unpaid watchman, a borrower, a paid watchman and a renter. What is the case?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the ברייתא it just brought and asks what case it is describing. This is a setup line that prepares the next two attempts.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא says the watchman pays half or full damages, but it does not say whose animal got hurt. The גמרא wants to know who the victim is, because that changes whether the ruling makes sense.

keyTerms.meaning: 'The Master said', the way the גמרא quotes a source it just brought in order to discuss it.
'What is the case?', a request to picture the exact situation.

phrases.english: The Master said:
"When it damaged, the one responsible for the damage is liable"
to include an unpaid watchman and the borrower,
a paid watchman and the renter.
What is the case?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens an analysis of the ברייתא brought in Step 26.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whose animal was hurt in the ברייתא's case, so that the half or full payment makes sense.

steps.title: It cannot be the lender's ox hurting the borrower's ox
steps.stepSummary: First attempt: the lender's ox, which the borrower was watching, hurt the borrower's own ox. This is rejected. The lender can say: if my ox had hurt anyone else's ox, you would have had to pay, so why should I pay you now?
steps.simpleTranslation: Suppose the lender's ox hurt the borrower's ox. Then let the lender say to him: 'If it had done damage out in the world, you would have had to pay. Now that it hurt your own ox, should I have to pay?!'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries the case where the animal being watched hurt the watchman's own ox, and the owner pays. It rejects this right away.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא says the watchman is the one responsible for the animal's damage. So if the borrowed ox had hurt a stranger's ox, the borrower would pay. It makes no sense that the owner should pay when the victim is the borrower himself, the very person who was supposed to be guarding it.

keyTerms.meaning: The lender, the owner who lent out his animal.
'Out in the world', meaning anyone else.
'If you say', an introduction to a suggested case.

steps.confusionAlert: Keep track of whose ox is whose. Here the attacking ox belongs to the lender but is in the borrower's care, and the ox that got hurt belongs to the borrower.

phrases.english: If you say that the lender's ox did damage
to the borrower's ox,
let him say to him:
phrases.notes: The lender is the one speaking, to the borrower.

phrases.english: If it had damaged out in the world,
you would have had to pay;
now that it damaged your own ox,
should I have to pay?!

steps.triggerLanguage: אִילֵימָא דְּאַזְּקֵיהּ תּוֹרָא דְמַשְׁאִיל לְתוֹרָא דְשׁוֹאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers the first possible answer to the question in Step 27 and knocks it down.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects reading the ברייתא as the owner paying the watchman for damage to the watchman's own ox.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The watchman would pay if a stranger were hurt, so the owner cannot owe him when he himself is the victim.

steps.title: It cannot be the borrower's ox hurting the lender's ox either
steps.stepSummary: Second attempt: the borrowed ox, which the borrower is responsible for, hurt the lender's ox. This is also hard. If a stranger's ox had hurt the borrowed ox, the borrower would have to pay for the whole ox. So why does the ברייתא say a תם pays only half?
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, the borrower's ox hurt the lender's ox. Then let the lender say to him: 'If my ox had been hurt by anyone else, you would have had to pay for the whole ox. Now that your ox hurt it, you pay me only half the damage?!'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא flips the case: now the borrower's ox hurt the lender's ox. This also runs into a problem with the ברייתא's half-damages ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A borrower has to pay the owner the full value of the borrowed ox if it gets hurt, even by an outsider. So when the borrower's own ox did the hurting, it is strange that he would pay only half damages just because his ox is a תם. Neither case fits the ברייתא yet. The next step answers this by going back to the first case.

keyTerms.meaning: Half damages, the payment for a תם.
Was damaged or hurt.
The whole ox, meaning its full value.

steps.whatToRemember: Both first attempts at picturing the ברייתא run into trouble. If the owner pays the watchman, he could say the watchman is responsible. If the watchman pays the owner, half damages is too little for a borrower. The next step rescues the first case.

phrases.english: Rather, the borrower's ox did damage
to the lender's ox,
let him say to him:
If it had been hurt by anyone else,
you would have had to pay for the whole ox;
now that your own ox hurt it,
you pay me only half the damage?!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא דְּאַזְּקֵיהּ תּוֹרָא דְשׁוֹאֵל לְתוֹרָא דְמַשְׁאִיל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After Step 28 failed, the גמרא tries the opposite case, and it is also challenged.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's ruling that a watchman whose ox is a תם pays only half damages.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A borrower must pay the full value if the borrowed ox is hurt by anyone. So paying only half when his own ox did the hurting does not make sense.

steps.title: Back to the first case: the borrower only agreed to guard the ox's body
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא goes back to the first case: the lender's ox hurt the borrower's ox. It says the ברייתא is talking about a borrower who took responsibility only for guarding the body of the lender's ox.
steps.simpleTranslation: Really, the case is where the lender's ox hurt the borrower's ox. What exact case are we dealing with here? Where the borrower agreed to guard the ox's body.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא returns to the first case it turned down in step 28 and saves it by making the case narrower. The borrower here agreed only to guard the ox's body.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 28 the lender said: if my ox had hurt anyone else, you would have paid, so why should I pay you? That only works if the borrower had taken responsibility for damage the ox does. Here the borrower only took responsibility for guarding the ox's body, so the lender's argument loses its force.

keyTerms.meaning: Really / actually. Used when the גמרא goes back to an idea it seemed to drop.
What case are we dealing with here? Used to narrow a ruling to one specific situation.
Guarding its body: taking responsibility so the animal itself does not get hurt or lost.
The lender, the owner who lent out his ox.
The borrower.

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up two kinds of guarding. Guarding the ox's body means protecting the ox itself. Guarding against the damage the ox does is a separate job, and that second job is what the lender's argument in step 28 depended on.

phrases.english: Actually, it is where it injured
phrases.notes: The גמרא is going back to the first case from step 28, the one it had pushed away.

phrases.english: the lender's ox injured the borrower's ox
and with what are we dealing here?
where he took upon himself guarding its body
phrases.notes: "He" is the borrower, and "its body" means the lender's ox. The sentence goes on in the next words of the גמרא.

steps.triggerLanguage: לְעוֹלָם דְּאַזְּקֵיהּ תּוֹרָא דְמַשְׁאִיל לְתוֹרָא דְשׁוֹאֵל, וְהָכָא בְּמַאי עָסְקִינַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Both attempts to define the case had problems (steps 28-29). The גמרא now returns to the first attempt and fixes it by narrowing what the borrower agreed to.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case (הָכָא בְּמַאי עָסְקִינַן): it limits what kind of guarding the borrower took on.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We thought the borrower was responsible for everything about the ox, including damage it does. Then the lender could say 'you would have paid anyway' (step 28).
steps.terutzMaskana: The borrower only agreed to guard the ox's body. So the lender cannot push his own ox's damage onto the borrower, and the first case can stand.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The ברייתא is talking about the lender's ox hurting the borrower's ox, where the borrower took on only guarding the ox's body.
